topic: API, SDK, data model and configuration

notes.front: What is the OpenTelemetry specification?
notes.back: The component that describes the cross-language requirements and expectations for all OpenTelemetry implementations.
notes.explanation: Beyond defining terms, it defines the API, the requirements for implementing it, and the data side (OTLP and semantic conventions), so every language follows one rulebook.
notes.evidence: Describes the cross-language requirements and expectations for all implementations. Beyond a definition of terms, the specification defines the following:
notes.example: Like the rules of chess: every chess set, in any country, must follow them, though the pieces look different.

notes.front: What is the OpenTelemetry API?
notes.back: The cross-cutting public interfaces used for instrumentation: any part of an OpenTelemetry client imported into third-party libraries and application code.
notes.explanation: Because libraries and applications import it, it is the part that is mixed into other people’s code.
notes.evidence: API packages consist of the cross-cutting public interfaces used for instrumentation. Any portion of an OpenTelemetry client which is imported into third-party libraries and application code is considered part of the API.
notes.example: Like the standard wall socket: every appliance is built to plug into it, whoever supplies the electricity.

notes.front: What is the OpenTelemetry SDK?
notes.back: The implementation of the API provided by the OpenTelemetry project, installed and managed within an application by the application owner.
notes.explanation: The SDK is the OpenTelemetry SDK; it also has its own public interfaces, constructors and plugin interfaces, which are not part of the API.
notes.evidence: The SDK is the implementation of the API provided by the OpenTelemetry project. Within an application, the SDK is installed and managed by the application owner.
notes.example: Like the power station behind the wall socket: the homeowner chooses the supplier, and the appliances never need to know.

notes.front: At the highest level, how is the OpenTelemetry client architecture organised?
notes.back: Into signals, such as tracing, metrics and baggage, each a specialised form of observability.
notes.explanation: The signals share one common subsystem, context propagation, but function independently from each other.
notes.evidence: At the highest architectural level, OpenTelemetry clients are organized into signals. Each signal provides a specialized form of observability. For example, tracing, metrics, and baggage are three separate signals.
notes.example: Like a building’s utilities: water, power and gas are separate systems, though they share the same service ducts.

notes.front: In OpenTelemetry, what is a distribution?
notes.back: A customised version of an OpenTelemetry component: a wrapper around an upstream OpenTelemetry repository with some customisations.
notes.explanation: The docs stress that a distribution is not to be confused with a fork.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry docs, Concepts, “Distributions”, What is a distribution?
notes.evidence: A distribution is a customized version of an OpenTelemetry component. A distribution is a wrapper around an upstream OpenTelemetry repository with some customizations. Distributions are not to be confused with forks.
notes.example: Like a car dealer’s special edition: the same factory model, with a trim package and different default settings.

notes.front: In the OpenTelemetry specification, what is AnyValue?
notes.back: The specification’s general value type: a primitive, a homogeneous primitive array, a byte array, or an array or map of AnyValue.
notes.explanation: Arrays and maps may be nested to any depth, so it can represent the equivalent of a JSON object.
notes.evidence: Arbitrary deep nesting of values for arrays and maps is allowed (essentially allows to represent an equivalent of a JSON object).
notes.example: Like a box that may hold one item, a row of identical items, or more boxes inside it.

notes.front: In the OpenTelemetry specification, what is an attribute?
notes.back: A key-value pair whose key is a non-null, non-empty string and whose value is one of the types defined in AnyValue.
notes.explanation: Attributes are used across signals and resources, so these rules apply to all of them.
notes.evidence: An Attribute is a key-value pair, which MUST have the following properties: - The attribute key MUST be a non-null and non-empty string.
notes.example: Like a label on a jar: “contents: jam”, where “contents” is the key and “jam” the value.

notes.front: What are the OpenTelemetry SDK environment variables?
notes.back: A set of language-agnostic environment variables for common configuration goals.
notes.explanation: The docs note that support for them varies across languages, with a compliance matrix listing which each language supports.
notes.evidence: Environment variable configuration defines a set of language agnostic environment variables for common configuration goals.
notes.example: Like the same thermostat settings working in any make of boiler, as long as it supports them.

notes.front: What is declarative configuration in OpenTelemetry?
notes.back: Configuring the SDK with a YAML file instead of environment variables.
notes.explanation: The specification calls it more expressive and full-featured than the environment variable based scheme.
notes.evidence: Declarative configuration uses a YAML file instead of environment variables.
notes.example: Like handing a caterer a full written menu, instead of shouting a few choices through the kitchen door.

notes.front: Which OpenTelemetry component is a vendor-agnostic proxy that can receive, process and export telemetry data?
notes.back: The Collector.
notes.explanation: The components page says it can receive several formats, such as OTLP, Jaeger and Prometheus, and send data to one or more backends.
notes.evidence: The OpenTelemetry Collector is a vendor-agnostic proxy that can receive, process, and export telemetry data.

notes.front: Which OpenTelemetry component lets you use the OpenTelemetry API to generate telemetry in your language of choice and export it to a preferred backend?
notes.back: The language-specific API and SDK implementations.
notes.explanation: The components page adds that these SDKs let you incorporate instrumentation libraries for common libraries and frameworks.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry docs, Concepts, “Components”, Language-specific API & SDK implementations
notes.evidence: OpenTelemetry also has language SDKs that let you use the OpenTelemetry API to generate telemetry data with your language of choice and export that data to a preferred backend.

notes.front: Which OpenTelemetry component generates telemetry from popular libraries and frameworks, such as data about inbound and outbound HTTP requests from an HTTP library?
notes.back: Instrumentation libraries.
notes.explanation: The components page describes them as components that generate relevant telemetry from popular libraries and frameworks for supported languages.
notes.evidence: OpenTelemetry supports a broad number of components that generate relevant telemetry data from popular libraries and frameworks for supported languages. For example, inbound and outbound HTTP requests from an HTTP library generate data about those requests.

notes.front: Which OpenTelemetry component, where a language supports it, instruments your application without touching your source code?
notes.back: Zero-code instrumentation.
notes.explanation: The underlying mechanism depends on the language, but it adds the OpenTelemetry API and SDK capabilities to the application.
notes.evidence: If applicable, a language specific implementation of OpenTelemetry provides a way to instrument your application without touching your source code.

notes.front: Which OpenTelemetry component is an implementation of a Kubernetes Operator that manages the Collector and the auto-instrumentation of workloads?
notes.back: The Kubernetes operator (the OpenTelemetry Operator).
notes.explanation: The components page lists it as one of OpenTelemetry’s main components.
notes.evidence: The OpenTelemetry Operator is an implementation of a Kubernetes Operator. The operator manages the OpenTelemetry Collector and auto-instrumentation of the workloads using OpenTelemetry.

notes.front: Which OpenTelemetry component provides pre-built Lambda layers to monitor functions run by cloud vendors?
notes.back: The Function as a Service assets.
notes.explanation: The components page says the community provides layers that auto-instrument your application, plus a standalone Collector layer.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry docs, Concepts, “Components”, Function as a Service assets
notes.evidence: The OpenTelemetry community currently provides pre-built Lambda layers able to auto-instrument your application as well as the option of a standalone Collector Lambda layer

notes.front: Which OpenTelemetry component sends telemetry to the Collector, or to a backend where you can visualise it?
notes.back: Exporters.
notes.explanation: The components page adds that using the Collector in production environments is a best practice.
notes.evidence: Send telemetry to the OpenTelemetry Collector to make sure it’s exported correctly. Using the Collector in production environments is a best practice. To visualize your telemetry, export it to a backend

notes.front: Which OpenTelemetry component is listed for supplying the resource, the entity producing telemetry, such as a process’s Pod name and namespace?
notes.back: Resource detectors.
notes.explanation: The components page describes them through the resource they fill in, using a process in a container on Kubernetes as the example.
notes.evidence: A resource represents the entity producing telemetry as resource attributes. For example, a process that produces telemetry that is running in a container on Kubernetes has a Pod name, a namespace,

notes.front: Which OpenTelemetry component provides the mechanism that moves data between services and processes?
notes.back: Cross-service propagators.
notes.explanation: The components page says propagation is not limited to tracing, but lets traces build causal information across services.
notes.evidence: Propagation is the mechanism that moves data between services and processes. Although not limited to tracing, propagation allows traces to build causal information about a system across services

notes.front: Which OpenTelemetry component restricts the amount of traces a system generates?
notes.back: Samplers.
notes.explanation: The components page says each language-specific implementation offers several head samplers.
notes.evidence: Sampling is a process that restricts the amount of traces that are generated by a system. Each language-specific implementation of OpenTelemetry offers several head samplers.

notes.front: Besides the API and the SDK, what does the specification’s “Data” part define?
notes.back: OTLP and vendor-agnostic semantic conventions that a telemetry backend can support.
notes.explanation: The specification covers three areas: the API, the SDK and the data.
notes.evidence: Data: Defines the OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) and vendor-agnostic semantic conventions that a telemetry backend can provide support for.

notes.front: A new language implementation of OpenTelemetry is being written. Where does its team look for the requirements every implementation must meet?
notes.back: C: the OpenTelemetry specification.
notes.choices:
A) The instrumentation registry
B) A vendor’s distribution
C) The OpenTelemetry specification
notes.choicesExplained: A lists instrumentation libraries for users to find, not requirements. B is one vendor’s customised version of a component, not the cross-language rulebook.
notes.explanation: The specification describes the cross-language requirements and expectations for all implementations.
notes.evidence: Describes the cross-language requirements and expectations for all implementations.

notes.front: Which OpenTelemetry packages may instrumentation authors reference directly?
notes.back: Only the API; they must not directly reference any SDK package.
notes.explanation: The specification states this as a hard requirement for instrumentation authors.
notes.evidence: Instrumentation authors MUST NOT directly reference any SDK package of any kind, only the API.

notes.front: The SDK has two kinds of public interfaces that are not part of the API. Who uses the SDK constructors, and who uses the SDK plugin interfaces?
notes.back: Application owners use the constructors; plugin authors use the plugin interfaces.
notes.explanation: These interfaces are not cross-cutting concerns, which is why the specification keeps them out of the API package.
notes.evidence: Note that the SDK includes additional public interfaces which are not considered part of the API package, as they are not cross-cutting concerns. These public interfaces are defined as constructors and plugin interfaces. Application owners use the SDK constructors; plugin authors use the SDK plugin interfaces.

notes.front: In general, what is the Trace API when no SDK is installed?
notes.back: A “no-op” API: operations on a tracer or on spans have no side effects and do nothing.
notes.explanation: The trace API specification states this as the general rule, with one exception it goes on to describe.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry specification, “Tracing API”, Behavior of the API in the absence of an installed SDK
notes.evidence: In general, in the absence of an installed SDK, the Trace API is a “no-op” API. This means that operations on a Tracer, or on Spans, should have no side effects and do nothing.

notes.front: A command-line tool uses a library that calls the OpenTelemetry Trace API, but the tool’s owner never installs an SDK. What happens to the library’s span calls?
notes.back: A: they have no side effects and do nothing.
notes.choices:
A) They have no side effects and do nothing
B) They throw an error until an SDK is installed
C) They send spans over OTLP to a default endpoint
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the API is designed to work, as a no-op, without an SDK. C needs an SDK with an exporter; the API alone exports nothing.
notes.explanation: Without an installed SDK the Trace API is, in general, a no-op, so the calls are harmless.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry specification, “Tracing API”, Behavior of the API in the absence of an installed SDK
notes.evidence: In general, in the absence of an installed SDK, the Trace API is a “no-op” API.

notes.front: An application’s owner wants its telemetry sent to a different backend. Its libraries use only the OpenTelemetry API. Where is the change made?
notes.back: B: in the SDK the application owner installs and configures.
notes.choices:
A) In each library’s instrumentation code
B) In the SDK the application owner installs and configures
C) In the OpenTelemetry specification
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: libraries use only the API and must not reference the SDK. C sets requirements for all implementations; it is not where one application is configured.
notes.explanation: The application owner installs and manages the SDK and uses its constructors, and exporting is defined on the SDK side.
notes.evidence: Within an application, the SDK is installed and managed by the application owner.

notes.front: Why does the specification call OpenTelemetry a cross-cutting concern?
notes.back: Because it is mixed into many other pieces of software in order to provide value.
notes.explanation: The specification says this is why client design needs extra care, to avoid creating issues for codebases that depend on these APIs.
notes.evidence: This makes OpenTelemetry a cross-cutting concern - a piece of software which is mixed into many other pieces of software in order to provide value.

notes.front: In the OpenTelemetry client architecture, what subsystem do all signals share, and how do they otherwise function?
notes.back: Context propagation; otherwise they function independently from each other.
notes.explanation: The specification names context propagation as the one common subsystem across signals.
notes.evidence: Signals share a common subsystem – context propagation – but they function independently from each other.

notes.front: In the OpenTelemetry client architecture, each signal consists of four types of packages: API, SDK, Semantic Conventions and {{c1::Contrib}}.
notes.back: Contrib
notes.explanation: The specification splits each signal this way to separate the cross-cutting parts that must be imported from the parts that can be managed independently.
notes.evidence: To accomplish these goals, each signal consists of four types of packages: API, SDK, Semantic Conventions, and Contrib.

image.alt: A grid with three signal columns, tracing, metrics and baggage. Each column has four package types stacked: API (cross-cutting), SDK (implements the API), Semantic Conventions and Contrib. Beneath all three columns runs one shared bar labelled context propagation, a common subsystem shared by all signals.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from the OpenTelemetry specification, Overview, OpenTelemetry Client Architecture

notes.front: An optional exporter plugin, separate from the SDK and not defined by the specification, sends telemetry to a popular analysis tool. The OpenTelemetry project maintains it. Which package type is it?
notes.back: C: a Contrib package.
notes.choices:
A) An API package
B) A semantic conventions package
C) A Contrib package
notes.choicesExplained: A holds the cross-cutting interfaces used for instrumentation, not exporting plugins. B holds the keys and values that describe common concepts, not plugins.
notes.explanation: The specification calls optional plugins that are separate from the SDK and maintained by the OpenTelemetry project Contrib packages; plugins it defines itself, such as OTLP exporters, are Core packages instead.
notes.evidence: Example SDK integrations include plugins for exporting telemetry to popular analysis tools and telemetry storage systems.

notes.front: How do core packages differ from contrib packages?
notes.back: Core packages implement specification-defined components and are maintained by an OpenTelemetry SIG; contrib packages are optional integrations.
notes.explanation: Core is not an extra package type; the term covers API, SDK and plugin packages such as exporters and propagators.
notes.evidence: Core packages are maintained by an OpenTelemetry SIG and are distinct from Contrib packages, which are optional.

notes.front: What are two kinds of customisation a distribution may include?
notes.back: Any two of: scripts to ease or customise use for a backend or vendor; changed default settings; additional packaging options.
notes.explanation: The docs list these as what a distribution’s customisations may include.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry docs, Concepts, “Distributions”, What is a distribution?
notes.evidence: Customizations in a distribution may include: - Scripts to ease use or customize use for a specific backend or vendor - Changes to default settings required for a backend, vendor, or end-user - Additional packaging options that may be vendor or end-user specific

notes.front: A vendor wraps the upstream OpenTelemetry Java agent, changes its default settings to suit its backend, and ships it as its own package. What is this?
notes.back: A: a distribution.
notes.choices:
A) A distribution
B) A fork
C) A contrib package
notes.choicesExplained: B is what the docs say a distribution must not be confused with; this one wraps upstream rather than splitting from it. C is an optional project-maintained integration, not a vendor’s wrapped build.
notes.explanation: A distribution is a wrapper around an upstream OpenTelemetry repository with some customisations, such as changed default settings.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry docs, Concepts, “Distributions”, What is a distribution?
notes.evidence: A distribution is a wrapper around an upstream OpenTelemetry repository with some customizations. Distributions are not to be confused with forks.

notes.front: In the signal lifecycle, in which status do signals start, and what may happen while they are in it?
notes.back: Development; breaking changes and performance issues may occur.
notes.explanation: The specification adds that a signal in Development may even be discarded and removed entirely.
notes.evidence: Signals start in Development status. While signals are in development, breaking changes and performance issues MAY occur.

notes.front: Which signal lifecycle status is reached after rigorous testing, and allows long-term dependencies to be taken?
notes.back: Stable.
notes.explanation: Long-term dependencies should not be taken against signals in Development, so reaching Stable is what makes them safe.
notes.evidence: Once a signal in Development has gone through rigorous testing, it MAY transition to Stable. Long-term dependencies MAY now be taken against this signal.

notes.front: Which signal lifecycle status marks a signal that has been replaced, and what support must its code keep?
notes.back: Deprecated; its code must keep the same support guarantees as stable code.
notes.explanation: The specification says signals may eventually be replaced, and are then marked as deprecated.
notes.evidence: Signals MAY eventually be replaced. When this happens, they are marked as deprecated. Signals MUST NOT be marked as deprecated unless the replacement is stable. Deprecated code MUST abide by the same support guarantees as stable code.

notes.front: Which signal lifecycle status ends support, and what version bump must the release make?
notes.back: Removed; the release must make a major version bump.
notes.explanation: Support ends when the signal is removed from the release.
notes.evidence: Support is ended by the removal of a signal from the release. The release MUST make a major version bump when this happens.

notes.front: When a signal’s components become stable, which one must become stable before the others?
notes.back: The API.
notes.explanation: Components may become stable together or one by one, but the API must lead.
notes.evidence: All signal components MAY become stable together, or MAY transition to stability component-by-component. The API MUST become stable before the other components.

notes.front: A new replacement for an existing stable signal is still in Development. May the existing signal be marked as deprecated now?
notes.back: B: no; not until the replacement is stable.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, as soon as the replacement exists
B) No; not until the replacement is stable
C) Yes, but only with a major version bump
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the rule that the replacement must be stable first. C confuses deprecation with removal, which is what needs the major version bump.
notes.explanation: The specification says signals must not be marked as deprecated unless the replacement is stable.
notes.evidence: Signals MUST NOT be marked as deprecated unless the replacement is stable.

notes.front: Your team is choosing a signal to build a long-lived production feature on. One signal is in Development, one is Stable. Which should you depend on?
notes.back: B: the Stable signal.
notes.choices:
A) The Development signal, as it is newer
B) The Stable signal
C) Either; they have the same guarantees
notes.choicesExplained: A risks breaking changes, or the signal being discarded entirely. C is wrong: Development carries no stability guarantees.
notes.explanation: Long-term dependencies should not be taken against signals in Development, but may be taken against a Stable one.
notes.evidence: In some cases, the signal in Development MAY be discarded and removed entirely. Long-term dependencies SHOULD NOT be taken against signals in Development.

notes.front: Are the attribute keys Region and region treated as the same key?
notes.back: No; case is preserved, so keys that differ in casing are distinct.
notes.explanation: The specification makes case sensitivity one of the required properties of an attribute key.
notes.evidence: Case sensitivity of keys is preserved. Keys that differ in casing are treated as distinct keys.

notes.front: Which of these would not be a valid OpenTelemetry attribute?
notes.back: C: a pair with an empty string as its key.
notes.choices:
A) Key http.route with a string value
B) Key retry.count with a 64-bit integer value
C) An empty string key with the value true
notes.choicesExplained: A and B each have a non-empty string key and a value of an AnyValue primitive type, so both are valid.
notes.explanation: The attribute key must be a non-null and non-empty string.
notes.evidence: The attribute key MUST be a non-null and non-empty string.

notes.front: May a homogeneous array in AnyValue mix a string and an integer?
notes.back: No; a homogeneous array must not contain values of different types.
notes.explanation: The definition of a homogeneous array is an array of primitive values of one type.
notes.evidence: a homogeneous array of primitive type values. A homogeneous array MUST NOT contain values of different types.

notes.front: What are two of the primitive types AnyValue allows?
notes.back: Any two of: string, boolean, double-precision floating point, signed 64-bit integer.
notes.explanation: These four are the primitive types; the other AnyValue forms are built from them.
notes.evidence: AnyValue is either: - a primitive type: string, boolean, double precision floating point (IEEE 754-1985), or signed 64 bit integer,

notes.front: Why should an SDK limit attributes?
notes.back: Without limits, erroneous code can create attributes that quickly exhaust memory, causing crashes that are hard to recover from safely.
notes.explanation: The specification says that by default an SDK should apply truncation, using configurable limits.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry specification, “Common specification concepts”, Attribute Limits
notes.evidence: Execution of erroneous code can result in unintended attributes. If there are no limits placed on attribute collections, they can quickly exhaust available memory, resulting in crashes that are difficult to recover from safely.

notes.front: If an SDK sets an attribute value length limit, what must it do with a string value that exceeds it?
notes.back: Truncate it so its length is at most the limit, counting each character as 1.
notes.explanation: Truncation keeps the attribute but caps how much memory it can take.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry specification, “Common specification concepts”, Attribute Limits
notes.evidence: if it is a string, if it exceeds that limit (counting any character in it as 1), SDKs MUST truncate that value, so that its length is at most equal to the limit,

notes.front: Over which two transports is OTLP implemented, and what schema do its payloads use?
notes.back: gRPC and HTTP; the payloads use a Protocol Buffers schema.
notes.explanation: The OTLP specification defines both transports around the same Protocol Buffers messages.
notes.evidence: is implemented over gRPC and HTTP transports and specifies Protocol Buffers schema that is used for the payloads.

notes.front: Which OTLP/HTTP payload encoding requires the header Content-Type: application/x-protobuf?
notes.back: Binary Protobuf encoding.
notes.explanation: OTLP/HTTP payloads are Protobuf, encoded either in binary format or in JSON format; this header marks the binary form.
notes.evidence: Binary Protobuf encoded payloads use proto3 encoding standard. The client and the server MUST set “Content-Type: application/x-protobuf” request and response headers when sending binary Protobuf encoded

notes.front: Which OTLP/HTTP payload encoding uses the proto3 standard JSON Mapping?
notes.back: JSON Protobuf encoding.
notes.explanation: The Protobuf schema of the messages stays the same whichever encoding is used.
notes.evidence: JSON Protobuf encoded payloads use proto3 standard defined JSON Mapping

notes.front: The default network port for OTLP/gRPC is {{c1::4317}}.
notes.explanation: It is also the port in the default gRPC endpoint, http://localhost:4317.
notes.evidence: default network port for OTLP/gRPC is 4317.

notes.front: The default network port for OTLP/HTTP is {{c1::4318}}.
notes.explanation: It is also the port in the default HTTP endpoint, http://localhost:4318.
notes.evidence: default network port for OTLP/HTTP is 4318.

notes.front: A firewall must let an application send OTLP/HTTP to a receiver listening on the default port. Which port must be opened?
notes.choicesExplained: A is the default port for OTLP/gRPC, not OTLP/HTTP. C is not an OTLP default port.
notes.explanation: The default port for OTLP/HTTP is 4318; 4317 is the default for OTLP/gRPC.
notes.evidence: default network port for OTLP/HTTP is 4318.

notes.front: What should an OTLP/HTTP client using HTTP/2 do if an HTTP/2 connection cannot be established?
notes.back: Fall back to HTTP/1.1.
notes.explanation: Implementations may use HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, and those using HTTP/2 should fall back.
notes.evidence: Implementations MAY use HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 transports. Implementations that use HTTP/2 transport SHOULD fallback to HTTP/1.1 transport if HTTP/2 connection cannot be established.

notes.front: An OTLP server accepts only part of the spans in a request. How does its response report the rest?
notes.back: It sends the same response message as for full success, setting rejected_spans to the number of spans it rejected.
notes.explanation: The specification uses the matching rejected_data_points and rejected_log_records fields for metrics and logs.
notes.evidence: If the request is only partially accepted (i.e. when the server accepts only parts of the data and rejects the rest), the server response MUST be the same Export<signal>ServiceResponse message as in the Full Success case.

notes.front: An OTLP server cannot keep up with the data it receives. What should it do, and what must the client then do?
notes.back: Signal backpressure to the client; the client must throttle itself to avoid overwhelming the server.
notes.explanation: The specification says a gRPC server signals backpressure by returning an error with code Unavailable.
notes.evidence: If the server is unable to keep up with the pace of data it receives from the client then it SHOULD signal that fact to the client. The client MUST then throttle itself to avoid overwhelming the server.

notes.front: Which SDK configuration interface must cover all configuration, and which should every other mechanism be built on?
notes.back: The programmatic interface, both times.
notes.explanation: The specification says it should be written in the language of the SDK itself.
notes.evidence: The SDK MUST provide a programmatic interface for all configuration. This interface SHOULD be written in the language of the SDK itself. All other configuration mechanisms SHOULD be built on top of this interface.

notes.front: How does the specification compare declarative configuration with the environment variable scheme?
notes.back: Declarative configuration is more expressive and full-featured.
notes.explanation: Environment variables cover common configuration goals; declarative configuration goes further.
notes.evidence: Declarative configuration provides a mechanism for configuring OpenTelemetry which is more expressive and full-featured than the environment variable based scheme,

notes.front: A team builds a tool that reads a YAML file and turns it into a well-defined struct passed to the SDK’s builder class. Which configuration interface is the tool built on?
notes.back: A: the programmatic interface.
notes.choices:
A) The programmatic interface
B) The environment variables
C) The OTLP exporter
notes.choicesExplained: B is a separate set of language-agnostic variables, not what a file-to-struct tool feeds. C sends telemetry; it does not configure the SDK.
notes.explanation: The specification gives exactly this shape, a file transformed into a struct for the SDK builder, as a mechanism built on top of the programmatic interface.
notes.evidence: All other configuration mechanisms SHOULD be built on top of this interface. An example of this programmatic interface is accepting a well-defined struct on an SDK builder class.

notes.front: Does every language’s SDK support every SDK environment variable?
notes.back: No; support varies across languages, and a compliance matrix lists what each supports.
notes.explanation: The docs put this note at the top of the general configuration page.
notes.evidence: Support for environment-variable configuration varies across languages. For the list of variables supported by each language, see the environment variable compliance matrix.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · OpenTelemetry docs as of that date

notes.front: Which resource attribute does OTEL_SERVICE_NAME set, and what is its default value?
notes.back: service.name; the default is unknown_service.
notes.explanation: The resources page recommends setting it explicitly, in code or with this variable, because of that default.
notes.evidence: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME Sets the value of the service.name resource attribute. Default value: unknown_service
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · OpenTelemetry docs as of that date

notes.front: A Pod sets OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES="service.name=billing,team=payments" and OTEL_SERVICE_NAME="invoices". What is the service.name resource attribute?
notes.back: B: invoices.
notes.choices:
A) billing
B) invoices
C) unknown_service
notes.choicesExplained: A would be right only if OTEL_SERVICE_NAME were not set, since it takes precedence. C is the default, used only when no service name is given.
notes.explanation: If service.name is also provided in OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES, OTEL_SERVICE_NAME takes precedence.
notes.evidence: If service.name is also provided in OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES, then OTEL_SERVICE_NAME takes precedence.

notes.front: In what format does OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES take resource attributes, and what is its default?
notes.back: Comma-separated key=value pairs, such as key1=value1,key2=value2; the default is empty.
notes.explanation: Each pair becomes a resource attribute.
notes.evidence: Key-value pairs to be used as resource attributes. Default value: empty Example: export OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES="key1=value1,key2=value2"
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · OpenTelemetry docs as of that date

notes.front: You want every service in production to report its deployment environment as a resource attribute, without changing code. What do you set?
notes.back: A: OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=deployment.environment.name=production.
notes.choicesExplained: B would rename every service to production rather than add an environment attribute. C chooses propagators; it does not set resource attributes.

notes.front: An engineer sets OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT="http://collector:4317/v1/traces" for a gRPC exporter. What is wrong?
notes.back: A: gRPC endpoints must not have OTLP/HTTP signal paths appended.

A) gRPC endpoints must not have OTLP/HTTP signal paths appended
B) Port 4317 is the default for OTLP/HTTP, not gRPC
C) Signal-specific endpoint variables do not exist
notes.choicesExplained: B has it backwards: 4317 is the gRPC default. C is wrong: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT is a documented trace-only variable.
notes.explanation: The docs say not to append paths such as /v1/traces to gRPC endpoint values; gRPC exporters use the OTLP protobuf service method for each signal.
notes.source: OpenTelemetry docs, “OTLP Exporter Configuration”, Endpoint Configuration
notes.evidence: Do not append OTLP/HTTP signal paths such as /v1/traces, /v1/metrics, or /v1/logs to gRPC endpoint values; gRPC exporters use the OTLP protobuf service method for each signal after connecting to the configured target.

notes.front: When do the docs say declarative configuration is useful?
notes.back: When you have many configuration options to set, or want options that are not available as environment variables.
notes.explanation: Both cases are ones the environment variable scheme handles poorly or not at all.
notes.evidence: This approach is useful when: - You have many configuration options to set. - You want to use configuration options that are not available as environment variables.

notes.front: Which environment variable points the SDK to a declarative configuration file?
notes.back: OTEL_CONFIG_FILE.
notes.explanation: The getting-started steps are to save the YAML file, then set this variable to its path.
notes.evidence: Set the environment variable OTEL_CONFIG_FILE=/path/to/otel-config.yaml
